summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old female with a history of coronary artery disease, mitral regurgitation, and prior kidney and pancreas transplants was admitted for scheduled heart catheterization and transesophageal echocardiogram. She reported progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, and exertional chest discomfort. Admission labs showed acute kidney injury with creatinine rising from a baseline of 2.6–3.2 to 3.9, prompting cancellation of the catheterization due to high risk of requiring dialysis. Her lisinopril was stopped, and carvedilol and amlodipine were increased to manage hypertension and cardiac workload. She was prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain. Kidney ultrasound showed no acute obstruction but suggested possible urothelial thickening, though urine culture was not diagnostic. Her transplant function remained stable. She was discharged home after three days with follow-up arranged with cardiology and nephrology, with a focus on outpatient evaluation and respecting her preference to avoid dialysis.
problems: Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease
Medication adjustment due to renal impairment
